skill: Knowing the purpose of the Enterprise Project Structure for organizing and batch-scheduling multiple projects
question: What is the primary purpose of the Enterprise Project Structure (EPS) in P6?

options.label: A
options.text: A hierarchical structure for organizing all of an organization's projects (e.g., by division, region, or program) that enables portfolio-level rollups, filtering, security, and multi-project operations such as opening several projects together for combined scheduling

options.label: B
options.text: A single project's WBS, simply renamed for enterprise-level reporting

options.label: C
options.text: A list of enterprise-wide resource codes only

options.label: D
options.text: A security role assigned to individual users

explanation: The EPS is the top-level hierarchy that organizes every project in the database, distinct from any single project's internal WBS. It is also the structure P6 uses to determine which projects can be opened and scheduled together as a set (a prerequisite for honoring cross-project relationships).
reasoning: Confusing EPS with WBS is a common early-career error, since both are hierarchical structures, but EPS sits above and outside individual projects while WBS is internal to one project.
commonMistakes: Confusing EPS with WBS.
Not realizing EPS nodes are also used for portfolio-level security and reporting rollups.
p6Checks: Enterprise > Enterprise Project Structure to view/manage the EPS hierarchy.
Right-click at an EPS node (or use the Projects window) to open multiple child projects together for combined scheduling.

followUpQuestions.prompt: How does EPS-level security differ from project-level security?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands the EPS also controls who can see/access entire branches of the portfolio.

skill: Knowing that Project Codes categorize whole projects rather than individual activities
question: A portfolio manager wants to filter the EPS to show only projects tagged 'Region: Gulf' and 'Contract Type: EPC,' regardless of what activities exist inside each project. Which P6 feature is designed for this?

options.label: A
options.text: Activity Codes

options.label: B
options.text: Project Codes

options.label: C
options.text: Resource Codes

options.label: D
options.text: WBS Codes

explanation: Project Codes are attributes assigned at the PROJECT level within the EPS (e.g., Region, Contract Type, Client), used to categorize and filter entire projects for portfolio-level reporting and security. Activity Codes, by contrast, tag individual activities inside a single project and would not help filter which whole projects appear in a portfolio view.
reasoning: Distinguishing 'attributes of a project' from 'attributes of an activity within a project' is fundamental to using P6's coding structures correctly at the portfolio level.
commonMistakes: Confusing Project Codes with Activity Codes because both are called 'codes' and both support filtering.
Assuming WBS (which is internal to one project) could be used to filter across many projects.
p6Checks: Enterprise Data > Project Codes – define the code structure (e.g., Region, Contract Type).
Projects window – assign the relevant Project Code values to each project, then filter/group the EPS view by those codes.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Could an Activity Code with the same name ('Region') also exist inside individual projects? Would that cause confusion?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate recognizes the two coding systems are entirely independent, even if similarly named.

skill: Diagnosing why an activity code value doesn't carry over when an activity is copied into another project
scenario: A planner copies several activities, including their assigned 'Area' activity code values (e.g., 'Zone 3 – East Wing'), from Project A into Project B using copy/paste. After pasting, the activities appear correctly in Project B, but the Area code column shows blank for all of them, even though a code definition named 'Area' still exists in Project B's activity code list.
question: What is the most likely reason the code VALUES didn't transfer even though a code definition with the same name exists in both projects, and how would this be avoided going forward?
explanation: The most likely reason is that the 'Area' activity code is scoped at the PROJECT level (not Global or EPS level) in each project independently, so even though both projects happen to have an activity code named 'Area,' the specific VALUES (such as 'Zone 3 – East Wing') defined under Project A's project-level code are separate value records from whatever exists under Project B's project-level code – they don't automatically map across projects, so the pasted activities lose the assignment. To avoid this going forward, if this code genuinely needs to stay consistent across multiple projects, it should be defined as a GLOBAL (or EPS-level) activity code instead of a project-level one, since Global/EPS-scoped code values are shared and remain consistent across every project that can see them.
reasoning: Activity Codes in P6 can be scoped Global, EPS, or Project; only Global and EPS-scoped codes share the same underlying value list across multiple projects, while Project-scoped codes are independently defined per project even if their code names coincidentally match.
commonMistakes: Assuming a code definition existing in both projects means the values are automatically shared.
Not checking the code's scope (Global/EPS/Project) before diagnosing the cause as a copy/paste bug.
Recreating the value manually in Project B without addressing the root cause for future copies.
redFlags: Concludes this is a P6 copy/paste defect without checking the code's scope first.
p6Checks: Enterprise Data > Activity Codes – check the scope (Global, EPS, or Project) of the 'Area' code definition in both Project A and Project B.
If Project-scoped, compare whether the code's value list is actually shared or independently defined per project.
For codes intended to stay consistent across a multi-project program, define them as Global or EPS-scoped from the outset rather than Project-scoped.

followUpQuestions.prompt: The program has already been running for a year with this code as Project-scoped in 8 different projects. What would converting it to Global involve, and what would you check before doing so?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands a scope change mid-program is not necessarily trivial or risk-free and requires careful handling of existing values.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Would this same issue occur with a Resource Code assigned to the copied activities' resource assignments?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands the scope concept generalizes to other enterprise code types, not just activity codes.

dimensions.guidance: Explains why matching names doesn't mean shared values.

dimensions.name: practicalApplication
